entry: Any of several commercially important ray-finned fishes of the family [[Salmonidae]]. Salmon of the genera *Salmo* and *Oncorhynchus* are native to tributaries of the North Atlantic and North Pacific basins, respectively. Salmon are typically anadromous: they hatch in gravel beds of freshwater streams, migrate to the ocean as adults and return to their birthplace to spawn. Some populations are landlocked. Folklore holds that fish return to the exact stream of their hatching, and tracking studies have shown this to be mostly true. Norway is the world's largest producer of farmed salmon, followed by [[Chile]]. Salmon are also prized game fish, and several species have been introduced to the [[Great Lakes]], [[Patagonia]] and the [[South Island]] of New Zealand. Their migrations carry ocean-derived nutrients inland, feeding bears and other animals.

Genus of rod-shaped, gram-negative bacteria in the family Enterobacteriaceae, named after the American veterinary surgeon Daniel Elmer Salmon. It comprises two species, *S. enterica* and *S. bongori*. *S. enterica* has six subspecies and more than 2,500 serotypes, and the genus is a leading cause of foodborne illness. Most infections result from eating food contaminated with feces. Nontyphoidal serotypes are zoonotic and usually cause salmonellosis, a gastrointestinal illness that often resolves without [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]]. Typhoidal serotypes cause typhoid and paratyphoid fever, which can be life-threatening and requires intensive care, including antibiotics. The bacteria are facultative anaerobes, producing energy with [[Oxygen|oxygen]] when it is available and by fermentation when it is not.

Family of ray-finned fishes, the sole extant member of the suborder Salmonoidei, including [[Salmon|salmon]], [[Trout|trout]], char, graylings and whitefishes. It comprises 11 extant genera and over 200 species of coldwater predatory fish native to the subarctic and cool temperate Northern Hemisphere. Most are migratory, spawning in gravel beds of freshwater headstreams and spending their juvenile years in rivers and lakes. Many species are anadromous, and salmonids are considered keystone organisms because they carry marine nutrients into inland ecosystems. The family has three subfamilies: Coregoninae (whitefishes), Thymallinae (graylings) and Salmoninae (trout, salmon, char, taimens and lenoks). The earliest known salmonid fossil, *Sivulliusalmo alaskensis*, was described in 2025 from Alaska, while the earliest previously recorded was the Early [[Eocene]] *Eosalmo driftwoodensis*.

Latin American dance music genre influenced mainly by Caribbean traditions, especially those of [[Cuba]], [[Puerto Rico]] and the [[Dominican Republic]]. Most salsa songs are based on *son montuno* and *son cubano*, with elements of cha-cha-chá, bolero, rumba, mambo and [[Jazz|jazz]]. The word *salsa*, Spanish for "sauce," was originally a commercial label for several styles of Hispanic Caribbean music, and its origin remains disputed. The first self-identified salsa band, Cheo Marquetti y su Conjunto – Los Salseros, was formed in Cuba in 1955. In the 1970s, self-identified salsa bands were assembled mainly by Puerto Rican, Cuban and Dominican musicians in [[New York City]]. Key figures included [[Celia Cruz]], Willie Colón, Rubén Blades, Johnny Pacheco and Héctor Lavoe. A parallel Cuban style, songo, evolved into timba in the late 1980s.

State capital and most populous city of [[Utah]], U.S. (pop., 2020: 199,723). Founded in 1847 by Mormon pioneers led by [[Brigham Young]], it grew through mining and the transcontinental railroad. Its metropolitan area has about 1.3 million residents. The city hosted the 2002 Winter Olympics and is known for skiing and its politically liberal culture. Record low water levels in the nearby Great Salt Lake have exposed arsenic that may become airborne, and two offshoots of the Wasatch Fault join beneath the downtown area.

Shallow, saline lake in Southern California, U.S., lying on the [[San Andreas Fault]]. It formed in 1905 when spring floods of the [[Colorado River]] broke through an irrigation canal and filled the Salton Basin. A resort destination in the 1950s and 1960s, it suffered fish and bird die-offs in the 1980s linked to rising salinity and farm runoff. Since 1999 the lake has shrunk as agriculture became more efficient and less runoff reached it, exposing lake bed that winds carry as toxic dust. In 2025, water began flowing into the first 2,000 acres of a 4,110-acre habitat and dust-suppression project.

Large crocodilian native to saltwater and brackish habitats from India's east coast to northern [[Australia]] and Micronesia, and the largest living [[Reptile|reptile]]. Males can reach 6 m (20 ft) and 1,000–1,500 kg (2,200–3,300 lb), while females rarely surpass 3 m (9.8 ft). An opportunistic [[Apex predator|apex predator]], it will prey on almost any animal entering its territory. It was hunted for its skin until the 1970s and has been listed as Least Concern since 1996. It is regarded as dangerous to humans.

Chilean socialist politician and 29th president of [[Chile]] (1970–73). A longtime member of the Socialist Party of Chile, he won the 1970 presidency as the candidate of the Popular Unity coalition after three unsuccessful campaigns. In office he pursued what he called "The Chilean Path to [[Socialism]]," nationalizing major industries and expanding education while clashing with the right-wing Congress and judiciary. On September 11, 1973, the military overthrew his government in a CIA-supported [[1973 Chilean coup d'état|coup]]. Declassified documents show that [[Richard Nixon]] and [[Henry Kissinger]] knew of the plans in advance. Allende died by suicide in his office that day, though the exact circumstances are disputed. Under [[Augusto Pinochet]], the regime persecuted alleged dissidents, and at least 3,095 civilians disappeared or were killed. Pinochet's rule ended after an internationally backed 1989 constitutional [[Referendum|referendum]].

Capital and largest city of the Brazilian state of [[Bahia]], on a peninsula between the [[Atlantic Ocean]] and the Bay of All Saints. Founded in 1549 by Tomé de Sousa, it was the first capital of colonial Brazil and is one of the oldest cities in the Americas. Its African heritage makes it a center of Afro-Brazilian culture. The colonial Historic Center, near the Pelourinho district, has been a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] since 1985, and the city belongs to UNESCO's Creative Cities Network as the "City of Music." Its carnival is among the largest in the world and, according to [[Guinness World Records]], the biggest street party in the world. With more than 2.4 million inhabitants as of 2020, it is the most populous municipality in Brazil's Northeast and the economic center of its state.

Spanish surrealist artist known for his technical skill and precise draftsmanship. Born in Figueres in [[Catalonia]], he trained in Madrid and joined the [[Surrealism|Surrealist]] group in 1929. His best-known work, *The Persistence of Memory*, was completed in 1931. He lived in France during the [[Spanish Civil War]] and moved to the United States in 1940, where he achieved commercial success. After returning to Spain in 1948, he developed a "nuclear mysticism" style. His output included painting, sculpture, film, photography and writing. His public support for the [[Francisco Franco|Francoist]] regime and his commercial activities have been controversial. His work influenced [[Pop art|pop art]] and contemporary artists such as Jeff Koons and Damien Hirst.

State of being saved or protected from harm or a dire situation. In religion, it generally refers to the deliverance of the soul from ignorance or perpetual harm. In [[Abrahamic religions]], salvation is the saving of the soul from [[Sin|sin]] and its consequences, attributed to God's grace, faith, good works or a combination of these. In [[Judaism]], redemption refers to God redeeming the people of Israel from exile, and adherents do not need personal salvation as Christians believe. In [[Christianity]], salvation is primarily achieved through faith in Jesus Christ. In [[Hinduism]] it is moksha, liberation from the cycle of rebirth, and in [[Buddhism]] it is [[Nirvana]], the extinction of desire and suffering.

Largest genus of plants in the mint family [[Lamiaceae]], with just under 1,000 species of shrubs, herbaceous perennials and annuals. Species are distributed across the Old World and the Americas, with about 600 in Central and South America and 250 in Central Asia and the Mediterranean. The name derives from Latin *salvia*, meaning sage. Two widely used herbs belong to the genus: common sage (*Salvia officinalis*) and [[Rosemary|rosemary]] (*Salvia rosmarinus*). The genus is defined by a staminal lever mechanism in which two stamens deposit pollen on a visiting pollinator. The Mexican *Salvia divinorum* contains the hallucinogen salvinorin A and is regulated in many countries.

Major river of [[Southeast Asia]] that flows from the [[Tibetan Plateau]] south through [[China]] and [[Myanmar]] to the [[Andaman Sea]]. It is known as the Thanlwin in Myanmar and the Nu Jiang in China. Only its last 90 km (56 mi) are navigable, where it forms a delta at Mawlamyine. The river runs through rugged mountain canyons and is one of the least fragmented large river systems in Asia, with only a few small dams. Its basin is considered one of the most ecologically diverse regions in the world. Since the 1970s, the Myanmar and Thai governments have sought to build large hydroelectric dams, while China dropped its plans for the upper river in 2016 in favor of a national park. Since Burmese independence in 1948, the basin has been a battleground in the [[Myanmar civil war (2021–present)|Myanmar civil war]].

Capital of the Austrian state of Salzburg, on the Salzach River near [[Germany]] (pop., 2026: 157,994). The city occupies the site of the Roman settlement of Iuvavum, became an episcopal see in 696 and a seat of the archbishop in 798. In the 17th century the [[Counter-Reformation]] brought many monasteries and [[Baroque architecture|Baroque]] churches. Its historic centre, a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]], is among the best-preserved city centres north of the [[Alps]]. The birthplace of [[Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart]], Salzburg is home to three universities.

American soul singer and songwriter often called the "King of Soul." During a thirteen-year career he released 29 singles that charted in the Billboard Hot 100 Top 40. He began as a gospel singer with the Soul Stirrers before turning to secular music in 1956. In 2015, [[Rolling Stone]] ranked him third among its 200 Greatest Singers of All Time. He was shot and killed by the manager of a motel in [[Los Angeles]]. Courts ruled the death a justifiable homicide, though his family has questioned the circumstances.

American general and statesman who played a prominent role in the Texas Revolution. He served as the first and third president of the [[Republic of Texas]] and as one of Texas's first two U.S. senators after annexation. He was also governor of [[Tennessee]] and of [[Texas]], the only individual elected governor of two different U.S. states. A veteran of the [[War of 1812]] under [[Andrew Jackson]], he opposed Southern secession and was the only Southern governor to refuse an oath of allegiance to the Confederacy. The city of [[Houston]] was named for him.

English filmmaker and stage director, knighted in 2020 by [[Elizabeth II]]. He won the Academy Award for Best Director for his first feature, *American Beauty* (1999). His other films include *Road to Perdition* (2002), *1917* (2019) and the James Bond films *Skyfall* (2012) and *Spectre* (2015). In theater he is known for dark re-inventions of musicals such as *Cabaret* (1993), *Oliver!* (1994) and *Company* (1995). He is developing four films on the lives of the members of [[The Beatles]].

American playwright, actor and screenwriter. He wrote 58 plays, marked by bleak, poetic and surreal elements and rootless characters on the outskirts of American society. *Buried Child* won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama, and he received a record 10 Obie Awards. Shepard also acted in films, including *The Right Stuff* (1983), for which he received an Academy Award nomination for best supporting actor. He died of [[ALS|amyotrophic lateral sclerosis]].

American business magnate best known for co-founding [[Walmart]] with his brother James "Bud" Walton. Walmart grew into the world's largest corporation by revenue, and Walton was the richest person in the United States from 1982 to 1988. Born in Kingfisher, Oklahoma, he earned a bachelor's degree in economics from the University of Missouri in 1940 and worked as a management trainee at J. C. Penney. He served in the U.S. Army during [[World War II]], after which he took over management of a variety store. He was also a philanthropist and a recipient of the Distinguished Eagle Scout Award from the Boy Scouts of America.

Largest city and administrative centre of Samara Oblast, [[Russia]], at the confluence of the [[Volga]] and Samara rivers. It is the ninth-largest city in Russia, with a population of over 1.14 million. Founded as a fortress in 1586 to guard the eastern frontier against nomads, Samara grew into a center of trade and diplomacy between Russia and the East, and [[Peter the Great]] visited it. The Volga has long been Russia's main commercial thoroughfare. Known as Kuybyshev from 1935 to 1991, it was formerly a closed city. Samara hosted the European Union–Russia Summit in May 2007. Its riverfront is a major recreation site for residents and tourists.

Silvery, moderately hard [[Lanthanide|lanthanide]] metal with symbol Sm and atomic number 62. Discovered in 1879 by French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, it was named after the mineral samarskite, from which it was isolated. It occurs in minerals such as monazite and bastnäsite, the main commercial sources, and China is by far the world's leading producer. Its main use is in samarium–cobalt magnets, whose compounds withstand temperatures above 700 °C (1,292 °F) without losing magnetism. The radioisotope samarium-153 is the active component of Quadramet, a drug that kills cancer cells in lung, prostate and breast cancers and in osteosarcoma. Samarium-149 absorbs neutrons and is added to [[Nuclear reactor|nuclear reactor]] control rods. Samarium has no biological role.

City in south-eastern [[Uzbekistan]], one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in [[Central Asia]] (pop., 2026: 882,000). Known as *Marakanda* when [[Alexander the Great]] captured it in 329 BC, it was a center of Sogdian civilization and a prosperous stop on the [[Silk Road]]. Samarkand was the capital of the Samanid Empire in the 9th century. In the 14th century [[Timur]] made it the capital of the [[Timurid Empire]], and it became a noted center of Islamic scholarship. Its Timurid monuments, including the Registan, the Gur-i Amir Mausoleum and the Bibi-Khanym Mosque, are known for cobalt and turquoise tilework. [[UNESCO]] listed the city as a [[World Heritage Site]] in 2001.

Umbrella term for Brazilian rhythms and musical genres of Afro-Brazilian origin, which emerged in [[Bahia]] in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The word originally designated a popular dance before it came to denote a musical genre. Modern samba was structured as a genre in the late 1920s in the Estácio neighborhood of [[Rio de Janeiro]], where samba schools and radio broadcasting helped establish urban Carioca samba. Once criminalized, samba became one of the main symbols of Brazilian national identity. Its traditional instruments include the pandeiro, cuíca, tamborim and surdo. In 2005, [[UNESCO]] declared Samba de Roda part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

Genus of 20 to 30 species of flowering plants in the family Viburnaceae, commonly called elders. Elders are mostly fast-growing shrubs or small trees bearing large clusters of small white or cream-colored flowers, followed by berries that ripen black, blue-black or red. Native to temperate and subtropical regions on most continents, they are widely cultivated for ornamental leaves, flowers and fruit. Raw berries, leaves and stems contain toxic cyanogenic glycosides, but cooked berries are edible and are used in jams, wines and syrups. The genus name derives from the Greek *sambūkē*, an ancient wind instrument.

Marriage of two people of the same legal sex or gender. As of 2026 it is legally recognized in 38 countries, with a total population of 1.5 billion. The first national law providing marriage equality was passed in the Netherlands in 2000 and took effect in 2001. Many jurisdictions that allow same-sex marriage also grant [[Adoption|adoption]] rights. Supporters, including major medical and scientific communities and [[Human rights|human rights]] organizations, cite research on the well-being of same-sex couples and their children. Opponents, mostly from conservative religious groups, argue that marriage is between a man and a woman.
